controls (college education, used to define power types of couples)

registers.name_in_paper: administrative data on an individual's labor market status at the end of a year
registers.role: treatment and controls (labor force participation in Denmark: employment, self-employment and unemployment; full-time work defined as more than 75% of the full-time equivalent)

registers.name_in_paper: own survey of emigrants from Denmark, carried out by Statistics Denmark in 2008
registers.role: outcomes (main motivation to emigrate, migration preferences, occupational position and labor force participation immediately after migration and in 2008)

linkages: survey answers linked to administrative records at the individual level using an anonymized identifier based on the social security number
male and female partners linked if married or living at the same address at the beginning of the year from which the survey sample was drawn
migrant couples identified in the migration register as both partners emigrating in the same year to the same destination with neither returning until the end of 2007

sample.universe: All couples in Denmark in 1987, 1988, 1992, 1993, 1997, 1998, 2001 or 2002 who were cohabiting or married, with both partners Danish citizens born in Denmark without immigrant background, aged 18 or above in the year of observation and at most 59 in 2007; and Danish emigrants of those years who had not returned by the end of 2007, surveyed in 2008
sample.unit_of_observation: couple-year in the register analysis; surveyed individual or couple in the survey analysis
selection_rules: both partners married or living at the same address at the beginning of the year
male-female couples only (no same-gender partnerships found among respondents)
both partners older than 18 on 1 January of the year of observation and at most 59 on 1 January 2007
both partners Danish citizens, born in Denmark and without immigrant background
migrant couples: both partners migrated within the same year to the same destination country and neither returned to Denmark until the end of 2007
couples having migrated to Greenland or the Faroe Islands excluded (autonomous territories of Denmark)
survey: emigrants aged 18 or older at emigration and at most 59 at the beginning of 2007, who emigrated in 1987/1988, 1992/1993, 1997/1998 or 2001/2002 and had not returned by the end of 2007
Tables 7 and 10 additionally require both partners to have stayed abroad together until 2008; couples in which both partners answered are included only once
dual-earner couples: both partners worked more than 75% of the full-time equivalent in the previous year
sample.n_observations: 4,474,254 couple-year observations in the all-couple emigration regressions; 1,888,022 among dual-earner couples (1,555,834 with a male primary earner, 331,305 with a female primary earner); 1250 migration events among all couples and 473 among dual-earner couples
sample.n_individuals: 1250 male and 1250 female partners in migrant couples in the administrative data; the survey reached 218 female and 213 male partners in 359 couples, about 10% of the 4257 survey respondents; 316 couples with both partners still together abroad in 2008

construction_notes: Labor force participation in Denmark follows the administrative data on an individual's labor market status at the end of a year and includes employment, self-employment and unemployment

Labor force participation abroad comes from the survey question on the respondent's or partner's occupational position; a partner is out of the labor force if the answer was 'spouse staying at home', retiree or student

Earnings are annual gross income from employment plus non-negative freelance income, measured in the year prior to the year of analysis, in Danish kroner and deflated using the consumer price index (base year 2000)
Earnings measures are only used for dual-earner couples in which both partners work more than 75% of the full-time equivalent in a given year

Power types follow Costa and Kahn (2000): power couples (both college educated), male/female power couples (only one partner college educated) and low power couples (neither); college education is defined as at least medium tertiary education in the register data, and in Table 10 according to the survey data in 2008
Destination groups: other Nordic countries, non-Nordic EU countries and Switzerland, the USA, and the rest of the world
In Table 8, couples are counted as having children immediately after emigration if the couple had a child registered already before emigration in Denmark

key_assumptions.supported_by: Statistics Denmark (2016); the migration register contains date of migration and destination

key_assumptions.assumption: The analysis conditions on both partners migrating together: couples in which only one partner emigrates are excluded because the administrative data cannot identify whether a cohabiting couple continues as a long-distance relationship or has broken up
key_assumptions.supported_by: survey questions on split migration identify only 18+22 such respondents

implies_edges.from: Both partners emigrating in the same year to the same destination

key_assumptions.assumption: Nonmigrant couples enter the data in each year they satisfy the restrictions while migrating couples enter only once; this lowers the estimated emigration probability but, the authors state, does not change any qualitative results
key_assumptions.supported_by: footnote 7: results remain robust if only requiring both partners among migrant couples to stay abroad at least 5 years

threats_discussed: nonmigrant couples appear in the data in every year they satisfy the restrictions while migrant couples appear only once, which lowers the estimated emigration probability
couples in which only one partner emigrates cannot be classified (long-distance relationship vs break-up) and are excluded
nonmigrant couples are included independently of whether they subsequently break up
